lede: Press a drawing pin and it sinks in; press the flat of your thumb just as hard and nothing happens. Pressure is a force spread over an area, and it is why a heavy tractor on wide tyres sinks less into a field than a person in stiletto heels.
can: Write pressure as force divided by area, and rearrange it.
Work out the area that is actually in contact.
Give the answer in the unit your numbers produce.

md: Pressure is the compound measure that says how **concentrated** a push is. The same weight on a wide base is gentle; on a narrow heel it dents the floor. The formula is short — $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$ — and all the work is in the $A$: which face is actually touching, and in which unit.

md:
Before you press a single button, write **area in contact = …**.

For a cube resting on a table, that is **one face**, not all six, and never the volume. For a drum standing on a floor, it is the **circle** underneath, $\pi r^2$. For a crate, it is the rectangle of its base.

The rest of the solid is irrelevant to the pressure it exerts, however tall or heavy it looks.

title: Why only the base counts
md: Pressure says how a push is shared out where two surfaces meet. The sides and the top of a crate touch nothing and carry none of the weight, so only the face resting on the floor goes into $A$.

prompt: A cube of side 5 cm rests on a table. What is the area in contact, in cm²?
explain: Yes: one face, 5 × 5 = 25 cm². The other five faces touch only air.

md:
From $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$ come the other two: $F = P \times A$ and $A = \dfrac{F}{P}$.

The unit follows the numbers you used. Newtons over square metres gives **N/m²**, which has a second name: the **pascal**, so $1$ N/m² $= 1$ Pa. Newtons over square centimetres gives **N/cm²**, and CCEA papers use both.

To move between them, remember that $1$ m² $= 100 \times 100 = 10\,000$ cm². Areas convert by the **square** of the length factor.

prompt: An area is 300 cm². How many square metres is that?
explain: Yes: 300 ÷ 10 000 = 0.03 m². A square metre holds 10 000 square centimetres.

title: Pressure
why: Four minutes of straight practice with the formula and its rearrangements. Watch which area is chosen in each example before the division happens.

prompt: A force of 0.35 N acts on every square centimetre of a foot of area 240 cm². What is the total force, in newtons?

md:
Two shapes come up again and again.

A **circular** base: the area is $\pi r^2$, so halve the diameter first. Summer 2025 saw candidates use the diameter as the radius, which makes the area four times too big.

A **square** base: if you have worked out the area and need the side, take the **square root**. Dividing by 4 is what you do to a perimeter, and it is the error both November 2025 reports named.

prompt: A square base has area 49 cm². How long is one side, in cm?
explain: Yes: √49 = 7 cm. Check it by squaring: 7 × 7 = 49.

title: Summer 2025, M3 Q19 and M4 Q6
md:
Part (a) asked for a volume or a surface area; part (b) asked for the **force** from a pressure. Many candidates carried their part (a) answer straight into part (b) even when it was a volume.
Treat each part as a fresh question: read what the formula needs, then go and get exactly that.

Write the area in contact down before anything else.
Use $P = F \div A$, or the rearrangement the question needs.
Give the answer in the unit your numbers produced.

Three marks, usually part (b) of a mensuration question. The first mark is the area in contact, written down and named; the second the substitution; the last the value, rounded as instructed, with its unit. Stuck: write down which face is touching and work out its area. If two objects exert the same pressure, find the pressure from the object you know completely first.
